results.corrected_extracted: People planning to attend a ceremony with a classic psychedelic (psilocybin mushrooms or truffles, ayahuasca, DMT, San Pedro, LSD or 1P-LSD) were recruited by online advertisements to a study website; eligibility: aged 18 or over, good English, and the intention to take part in a retreat, ceremony or other guided experience with a classic psychedelic. Survey links went out about a week before, one day after and 4 weeks after the indicated date, and the two main measures (the Metaphysical Beliefs Questionnaire and nine FAD-Plus free-will and fatalism items) were taken at baseline, 4 weeks and 6 months. Baseline table: N = 819, age 44.4 ± 12.6 (not labelled; presumably mean ± SD), 359 women (43.8%) and 455 men (55.6%), United States 43.8%, United Kingdom 19.5%, master's degree 33.6% and doctorate or professional degree 20.5%, White 90.7%, median household income 9000 dollars a month. Trial: 59 patients with major depression who completed a double-blind randomized trial (30 given two 25 mg doses of psilocybin and 6 weeks of daily placebo, 29 given two 1 mg doses and daily escitalopram), with an adapted questionnaire at baseline and 6 weeks; registered as NCT03429075.
results.note: All numbers match pp. 8-10 and Table 2. Only change: Table 2 prints age as 44.4 ± 12.6 without saying mean or SD, so the label is hedged.

results.corrected_extracted: 866 respondents are said to have completed the belief survey at different time points. The 13-item questionnaire (ten items written for the survey, three from earlier work) gave one factor of nine items, Non-physicalist Beliefs (Cronbach's alpha 0.86), loading positively on another realm that can be visited (0.790), a supernatural transition to such realms (0.740), a unifying principle beyond any material or scientific explanation (0.776), panpsychism (0.642), primacy of other realms (0.592), dualism (0.444) and the physical world as an illusion generated by consciousness or the mind (0.441), and negatively on materialism (−0.727) and naturalism (−0.598). The authors say the relation between items and philosophical positions could be contested, so the items are arguably best taken at face value.
results.note: Loadings, alpha 0.86 and 866 match Table 1 and p. 2. The source hedges the face-value point ('arguably best treated at face-value'); the hedge is restored.

All statistics match pp. 2-3 and Fig. 1a (Methods: two-tailed, Bonferroni-corrected). Recomputed d = t/√n for n = 122 and 53, and editors' intervals 0.148-0.512 and 0.273-0.647. Printed intervals fit CIs of the raw mean change.

results.corrected_extracted: Item means (with standard errors) at baseline lie on the agree side of neutral for ontological and supernatural transcendentalism, non-naturalism, panpsychism, primacy of other realms and dualism, and on the disagree side for materialism, naturalism and solipsism/idealism. Changes are marked as significant at 6 months (**) for ontological and supernatural transcendentalism, materialism (down), panpsychism and dualism, and at 4 weeks only (*) for non-naturalism and primacy of other realms; naturalism and solipsism/idealism carry no marker, although the legend lists solipsism/idealism among the items that shifted. The axis runs from Disagree to Agree without numbers, so item changes cannot be given in scale units.
results.note: Read at 300 dpi: baseline means for naturalism and solipsism/idealism also sit left of neutral (disagree side); the legend defines ** as a significant change at 6 months, not 'up to'. Markers otherwise as stated.

results.corrected_extracted: The authors call this the first study to show personality change in healthy adults after an experimentally manipulated discrete event and call for replication in larger groups with diverse baseline personalities; they compare the rise with the usual fall in Openness of about 1 T point per decade in normal ageing and with smaller rises after antidepressant treatment or intensive outpatient counselling, figures from other studies; and they write that differences in participants' motivation and preparation likely contributed to the different outcome of an earlier LSD study, and that it is possible that their regularly spiritually active participants are particularly sensitive to psilocybin's mystical-type effects, which predicted the Openness increases.
results.note: First two points confirmed. In the 4th paragraph the source says motivation and preparation 'likely' contributed (contrast with McGlothlin's LSD study) and calls spiritual sensitivity 'possible'; the merged 'may have contributed' blurred both.

results.corrected_extracted: No factor of the NEO PI-R personality inventory, and neither the positive nor the negative affect scale of the PANAS-X, was differentially affected by psilocybin: the two order groups (15 given psilocybin first, 15 methylphenidate first) did not differ significantly at screening or 2 months after session 1, and the methylphenidate-first group showed no significant change from after session 1 to after session 2, its psilocybin session. No values are shown.
results.note: The PDF is now on file (uploaded 14 Nov) and was checked: p. 278 says 'no significant differences' and 'no significant changes'; the anchor had dropped 'significant'. Update source_read.

results.corrected_extracted: Three adults nominated by each participant, interviewed by telephone 7 to 8 weeks after each session (N = 26), rated a mean positive change in the participant's behaviour and attitudes of 2.42 (SEM 0.70) after psilocybin against -0.03 (SEM 0.68) after methylphenidate (p < 0.01), which the authors call a small but significant positive change. The paper does not relate these ratings to the personality scores.
results.corrected_locator: Materials and methods › Community observer ratings of changes in participants' behavior and attitudes (p. 273); Table 4 and Results › Community observer ratings of changes in participants' and behavior and attitudes (heading as printed) (p. 278)
results.note: Checked in the PDF now on file: Table 4 values and N = 26 confirmed; the nomination and 7-8-week interview details are on p. 273. 'In the card' replaced by 'the paper'.

results.corrected_extracted: Of 36 enrolled (14 men), 30 were randomized to drug order (15 per order) and 6 to a decoy arm that had methylphenidate twice and then open-label psilocybin in a third session; the decoy arm's data were left out of the statistical analyses. MacLean et al. took 35 of these 36 into their analysis (one excluded for incomplete personality data) and describe every high-dose session as blinded, so their 35 would include at least five of the six open-label sessions (editors' inference).
results.corrected_locator: Materials and methods › Participants and Study design (p. 269); Instructions to participants and monitors, last paragraph (p. 271: these six third sessions were the only unblinded sessions)
results.note: Text confirmed in the PDF now on file; the locator pointed to the card, so a source locator is given. The inference holds: MacLean says neither participants nor monitors knew when the high dose came.

Limitations box (p. 368), Participants, Study procedure, Measures and Results 1st paragraph (pp. 369-370) match; the d formula on the rendered p. 370 is (baseline mean - 3-month mean)/((SD1)^2 + (SD2)^2)^0.5, no division by 2.
All domain values, signs (-5.7, d -0.571) and p values match Table 1 at 300 dpi and the Results text; 11 facets significant, 10 bold after FDR; no SDs printed.
Signs read on the rendered p. 371: -23 ± 17 vs -6 ± 8; r = -0.47, 0.54, 0.47. Units not stated; weighted means fit raw-score units (editors' inference). Exploratory, uncorrected per Methods p. 370.

results.corrected_extracted: Openness change did not correlate with treatment response or differ between responders and non-responders, which the authors call consistent with Openness being orthogonal to anxiety or depression symptoms (while noting some findings of a moderate relation with wellbeing) and take as support for the change potentially being in addition to, rather than a direct effect of, improved mood, citing their own unpublished survey (data not shown). Against d values they computed from three antidepressant trials (five samples, 469 patients, 8 to 20 weeks), Neuroticism, Agreeableness and Conscientiousness changed similarly (−0.59, 0.04 and 0.18 there; −0.57, −0.01 and 0.27 here), while Openness (0.44 against 0.13) and Extraversion (0.72 against 0.32) changed more; they advise caution because follow-up times differ. From these data, they write, it is hard to infer that the changes, in particular in Neuroticism and Extraversion, are trait rather than state changes, though a change lasting 3 months might suggest more than a state artefact.
results.note: All d values and signs confirmed on the rendered p. 373. The source hedges the Openness reading ('potentially being an addition to'); 'read as a change beyond improved mood' dropped that hedge.
Discussion 10th (p. 374), 12th (pp. 374-375) and 13th (p. 375) paragraphs say each point as given; 'probably less likely to volunteer' is kept as a suggestion.

key_findings.correction: Respondents having their first psychedelic experience (t(52), that is 53 people by the editors' reading of the degrees of freedom; the n is not printed) shifted more: d = 0.53 at 4 weeks (t(52) = 3.85, p = 0.001) and d = 0.73 at 6 months (t(52) = 5.32, p < 0.0001).

At the item level, Figure 1b marks a significant change at 6 months (**) for ontological transcendentalism, supernatural transcendentalism, materialism (down), panpsychism and dualism, and at 4 weeks only (*) for non-naturalism and primacy of other realms; naturalism and solipsism or idealism carry no significance marker. At baseline the means already lay on the agree side for the transcendentalism, non-naturalism, panpsychism, primacy and dualism items and on the disagree side for materialism, naturalism and solipsism or idealism.

reporting_issues.correction: issue: The Results say 866 respondents completed the belief survey at different time points, Table 2 gives 819 at baseline, and the paired analyses have 121 degrees of freedom (122 people) at both 4 weeks and 6 months; the abstract calls the sample large. | consequence: The headline belief shifts rest on about 15% of the baseline sample, and the main text does not say who the 122 were or how they compared with those who dropped out (Supplementary Table 1, cited for sample characteristics, was not read).

risk_of_bias.note: Agree with design (prospective cohort plus trial secondary analysis), ROBINS-E and overall very high: confounding by the ceremony context, missing data and selective reporting are each high.

interpretation_gap.note: Substantial: each of the six gaps checked against pp. 1, 3, 6, 8 and 11.

missed: Editors' inference supporting reporting issue 2: the smallest group sizes that fit all four printed percentages in each row of Figure 2a are 119 dualists, 45 materialists, 58 idealists and 142 none/mixed (364 at 4 weeks, close to the about 370 implied by Figure 3); at 6 months the rows fit 46 dualists, 24 idealists, 46 none/mixed and a multiple of 9 materialists. So 'hard materialist' percentages at 4 weeks plausibly rest on about 45 people.
design_detail calls the trial 'phase 2' and comparison.controls says both arms had psychological support; neither is stated in this paper (they come from the trial report, not read).
demographics: Table 2 prints age as 44.4 ± 12.6 without labelling it SD; and the main text cites Supplementary Table 1 for sample characteristics next to the 866, not as describing the 122 analysed.

selection_effects repeats the baseline reading of Figure 1b without naturalism and solipsism/idealism, whose baseline means are also on the disagree side; validity_norms drops the source's 'arguably' before 'best treated at face-value'.

key_findings.correction: Respondents with MEQ scores at or above the median reported larger increases than those below it; 'before' ratings were similar in the two groups, and at 'after' the groups differed meaningfully for every entity except other humans. The relationship held with MEQ as a continuous variable after adjustment for demographic, psychedelic-use and other variables including psychological challenge. Note: group sizes are not given; the main text gives no statistics or location for the adjusted model (Supplementary Table 3, which it cites for the low/high MEQ comparison, was not read).

risk_of_bias.note: Agree with design (retrospective survey), JBI prevalence checklist and overall high; selection on the outcome and recall of 'before' beliefs dominate.

interpretation_gap.note: Substantial; quotations and the four gaps checked on pp. 1, 5-6.

missed: The Results say agreement 'decreased monotonically' across entities in their assumed order, but Table 2 has plants above fungi at all three time points (26/21, 61/56, 64/62) and above insects after (61/57), and Figure 1's 'after' mean for fungi sits above insects (editors' reading at 300 dpi). Minor.

analysis.effect_sizes says the continuous-MEQ mixed model is reported only in Supplementary Table 3; the main text cites that table for the low/high MEQ comparison and gives no location for the model.

The abstract says findings were similar 'when restricted to' respondents reporting on their first psychedelic experience, while the Results describe only that effects were not affected by it (data not shown); the share whose reference experience was their first psychedelic experience of any kind is not reported (Table 1 gives 44% for first belief-changing experience).

key_findings.correction: The authors contrast their result with a controlled LSD study (McGlothlin et al., 1967) that found no significant improvement in creativity or aesthetic measures at 6 months, writing that differences in participants' motivation and preparation (paid graduate students with little interest in LSD and minimal support there, unpaid motivated volunteers with extensive preparation here) likely contributed to the different long-term outcomes, and that it is possible that spiritually active people are particularly sensitive to the mystical-type effects that predicted the Openness increase.

risk_of_bias.note: Agree with RoB 2 overall high and the reasoning that the card's estimates are within-person changes and experience-defined groups not protected by randomization; filing as crossover-rct is explained in design_detail.

missed: The parent Study 1 (Griffiths et al., 2006, p. 278; its PDF is now on file) reported that no NEO PI-R factor was differentially affected by psilocybin: the randomized order groups (15 and 15) did not differ significantly 2 months after session 1, and the methylphenidate-first group showed no significant change after its psilocybin session. This is the only randomized comparison of personality change in these data, and it was null (small groups, no values shown); cannot_establish and comparison should mention it.

At least five of the 35 Study 1 participants were Griffiths et al.'s decoy-arm volunteers, whose third, psilocybin session was unblinded (Griffiths 2006, pp. 269, 271), while this paper describes the high-dose session as blind to timing for all (editors' inference); relevant to RoB domain 2.

risk_of_bias.note: Agree with case-series (single-arm before-after), ROBINS-I and overall critical for a causal reading: no comparison group, unblinded self-report, extreme baseline scores.

interpretation_gap.note: Substantial. For fairness, the abstract itself qualifies the insightfulness 'prediction' as 'in an exploratory analysis' (p. 368); the claimed field and RoB domain 7 should say so.

missed: The abstract labels the insightfulness 'prediction' as exploratory ('predicted, in an exploratory analysis', p. 368); the card presents it as unqualified.

Table 1 prints negative d for falls (Neuroticism -0.571) although the printed formula (baseline mean minus 3-month mean) would give positive values; the signs follow the direction of change. Minor; could join reporting issue 0.
